summary: Specifies using CMAC mode with AES as an authentication mechanism for IPsec ESP and AH, under the name AES-CMAC-96. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A way for secure Internet tunnels to stamp each packet with a secret signature, using a scrambler most computers already have.

questions: how does aes-cmac-96 work with ipsec
how long is the aes-cmac-96 output
subtitle: How to use the AES block cipher to stamp IPsec packets with a 96-bit authentication tag.

tldr.problem: IPsec's ESP and AH protocols need a message authentication code, and some systems have the AES block cipher available more readily than a hash function.
tldr.mechanism: AES-CMAC-96 runs AES-CMAC with a 128-bit key over the message, then keeps only the 96 most significant bits (12 octets) of the 128-bit output.
tldr.outcome: It gives ESP and AH a MAC built from AES alone, and the 96-bit result matches the default authenticator length that AH specifies.

today: RFC 4494 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its algorithm builds on RFC 4493.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4494 specifies how to use CMAC, a Cipher-based Message Authentication Code from NIST, in the authentication mechanism of the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Authentication Header (AH) protocols. The new algorithm is named AES-CMAC-96.

The RFC traces the family tree. CMAC is equivalent to OMAC1, which improves on XCBC, which in turn improves on the basic CBC-MAC. XCBC addresses security deficiencies of CBC-MAC, and OMAC1 reduces the key size of XCBC.
sections.eli5: Grown-up computers need a way to sign every packet. This memo picks a signing method built on a scrambler called AES and says how to plug it into secure tunnels.

sections.title: Basic Definitions
sections.content:
The RFC defines a handful of symbols. The key K is a 128-bit (16-octet) key for the AES-128 cipher. The message M is what gets authenticated, and len is its length in octets. The minimum length is 0, and this document does not specify a maximum.

truncate(T,l) keeps the first l octets of the MAC T, taking bits in most-significant-bit-first order. AES-CMAC-96 is the IPsec MAC function that keeps the 96 most significant bits of the 128-bit AES-CMAC output.
sections.eli5: Before the recipe, the memo names its ingredients: a secret key, the message, and a rule for chopping the signature down to size.

sections.title: What AES-CMAC Provides
sections.content:
AES-CMAC is built on the AES block cipher and the CMAC mode of operation. The RFC says it gives stronger assurance of integrity than a checksum or error detecting code. A checksum detects only accidental changes, while CMAC is designed to detect intentional, unauthorized modifications as well as accidental ones.

The RFC says AES-CMAC achieves a similar security goal to HMAC. The difference is the building block: AES-CMAC uses a symmetric key block cipher, while HMAC uses a hash function such as SHA-1. So AES-CMAC suits systems where AES is more readily available than a hash function. It also notes that, according to NIST, at least 64 bits should be used against guessing attacks.
sections.eli5: A plain checksum only notices honest mistakes. This signature also catches someone sneaky changing the message on purpose.

sections.title: The AES-CMAC-96 Algorithm
sections.content:
For IPsec message authentication on AH and ESP, AES-CMAC-96 should be used. It is AES-CMAC with the output truncated to 96 bits in MSB-first order. The resulting 96-bit MAC meets the default authenticator length specified in the AH RFC.

The algorithm has two steps. In step 1, AES-CMAC is applied to the message M of length len with key K, giving T. In step 2, T is truncated to 12 octets and that truncated value is returned.
sections.eli5: First make a long signature. Then keep only the first part of it, like using just the first twelve letters of a long secret code.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC gives four test cases so implementers can check their work. They are the same as the ones in the NIST CMAC document, except that the outputs are truncated to 96 bits. All use the key 2b7e1516 28aed2a6 abf71588 09cf4f3c.

The messages have lengths 0, 16, 40 and 64 octets. For example, the empty message gives bb1d6929 e9593728 7fa37d12, and the 16-octet message gives 070a16b4 6b4d4144 f79bdd9d. The RFC also lists the two subkeys, K1 and K2, derived from the key.
sections.eli5: The memo includes answer-key examples, so you can check that your own signing program gets the same answers.

sections.title: ESP Interaction, Security and IANA
sections.content:
On interaction with the ESP cipher mechanism, the RFC says that as of writing there are no known issues that preclude using AES-CMAC-96 with any specific cipher algorithm.

Its security considerations section simply points to the security considerations of the AES-CMAC document, RFC 4493. For IANA, value 8 of the IKEv2 Transform Type 3 (Integrity Algorithm) registry was allocated to AUTH_AES_CMAC_96.
sections.eli5: The memo says it knows of no problems mixing this signature with any scrambler, and it borrows its safety notes from the parent document. It also got its own number in the official list.
